paragraphs.heading: Where air masses meet
paragraphs.text: A weather front is the boundary between air masses that differ in things like density, wind, temperature and humidity. Fronts divide air masses of different types or origins, and they lie along troughs of lower pressure. Because the two sides differ, the weather along the line is often unsettled. Some fronts bring hardly any cloud or rain, but the wind always shifts as one passes.

paragraphs.heading: Cold fronts
paragraphs.text: A cold front sits at the leading edge of the cooler air. Cold air is denser than warm air, so it both lifts and pushes the warm air ahead of it, and cold fronts can travel up to twice as fast as warm fronts. As moist warm air is lifted and condenses, it often forms a narrow line of showers and thunderstorms. Cold fronts usually travel from west to east, and on weather maps they appear as a blue line with triangles pointing the way the cold air moves.

paragraphs.heading: Warm fronts
paragraphs.text: A warm front sits at the leading edge of an advancing mass of warm air and usually moves toward the pole. It travels more slowly than the cold front that often follows, because the dense cold air ahead is harder to lift off the ground. The clouds that show up ahead of it are mostly of the stratiform kind, rain builds gradually as the front nears, and fog may form beforehand. Once the front passes, skies usually clear and warm quickly. Maps show it as a red line of half-circles pointing where the air is heading.

paragraphs.heading: Occluded and stationary fronts
paragraphs.text: When a cold front catches up with a warm front, the two merge into an occluded front, which usually forms around mature low-pressure areas such as cyclones. The cold and warm fronts curve toward the pole into the meeting spot, called the triple point. In a cold occlusion, the air arriving from behind is cooler than the cold air retreating ahead, and it ploughs under both. A stationary front, by contrast, is one that has stalled.

paragraphs.heading: Strong and weak fronts
paragraphs.text: Meteorologists use two terms for the weather around a front. An anafront is unstable: air climbs quickly along and over the boundary, bringing big changes and heavy precipitation. A katafront is weaker, with smaller shifts in temperature and moisture and only limited rain. In summer, gentler contrasts in humidity, called dry lines, can also set off severe weather.

paragraphs.heading: Finding fronts on a map
paragraphs.text: Fronts are tracked on surface weather analyses, maps that give a top view of the weather over an area at one moment, built from ground weather stations. Forecasters plot values like sea-level pressure, temperature and cloud cover to locate them. Mountains and bodies of water can also change how fronts move and behave. Over a uniformly warm ocean, for example, the density contrast can fade until the front becomes only a shear line, which simply divides areas with differing winds. This happens most often over the open ocean.
